newsitem.title: MALTA: Maltese turn out to vote in key polls.
newsitem.headline: Maltese turn out to vote in key polls.

text.p: Tens of thousands of people turned out in Malta on Saturday for a general election seen as a referendum on whether the Mediterranean island should pursue its bid to join the European Union.
In the politically conscious island, hundreds queued in bright sunshine at booths in the fortress capital, Valletta.

There were no official figures on turnout but one electoral officer said: "It's been running about the same as last time as far as one can tell." For the past four elections, turnout has topped 94 percent, and in 1992 totalled 96.04 percent.
Queues formed as booths opened, several up to 35 minutes late. Many of the early voters were women, including groups of brown-habited nuns.
The election has been described by Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami as a "sort of another referendum on Malta's 1990 application to join the EU".

Opposition Labour Party leader Alfred Sant opposes EU membership, saying it is inapplicable for the small island. He has pledged to seek a "special relationship" with Europe and "positive neutrality" for Malta.

He is also pinning his hopes of overturning the Nationalist Party's record 13,000 vote majority of 1992 on discontent with VAT (Value Added Tax) which he says has caused hardship to the Maltese and was imposed purely to prepare for Europe.
He is pledged to scrap it, killing Malta's 1990 application for EU membership, and to replace it with customs tariffs.
Divided into two mainstream parties, only 5,000 votes have normally decided victory or defeat in the island's electorate of 275,000.

Fenech Adami, 62, who has a three-seat majority in the 65- member parliament, said on Friday: "I already have a mandate... (but) it will be a sort of another referendum on Malta's membership of the EU."
Sant, 48, said: "We should have a special relationship, not membership...I would like to see security, not military, cooperation, for example on drugs, contraband and the movement of people."

"The Nationalists have brought us tranquillity and security and should be allowed to go ahead with their policies," one middle aged businesswoman, who asked not to be identified, said as she queued to vote.
Her friend, a young shop manageress who also did not give her name, said she would vote for Labour because she trusted Sant and believed his ideas would help ordinary people.

At campaign meetings, the Nationalist Party has boasted of its management of the economy, based mainly on manufacturing and tourism. It points to economic growth of some six percent a year with unemployment reduced to 3.2 percent.
"We will be able to open our doors without restriction to a market of 314 million people," said Fenech Adami, who sees EU talks completed and Malta ready for membership by mid-1998 .
His party adds: "The price Malta will have to pay for the withdrawal of its application for membership is far too great."
Labour, long uneasy about increased visits to the island by Western naval ships, is also committed to pulling Malta out of NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme which it joined in 1995.
Malta has no independent opinion polls and few will forecast the outcome of Saturday's poll.

Political correspondent Anthony Manduca of the Malta Independent, said: "There is a possibility that no major party will achieve an absolute majority of votes...which has not happened in Malta since 1966."

The 'wild card' could be the Democratic Alternative which won no seats in 1992. It favours EU membership in principle but says a referendum should take a final decision after all conditions are known.
Polling stations close at 10 p.m. Counting starts shortly after but with a complex vote system results are not expected until late on Sunday or early on Monday.
